docs.hudButton.component: A BUTTON is one literal of data assembled into an element — the same bargain `pile()` strikes,
for the other thing every game grows: undo, restart, a hint, end turn, a settings gear.
```ts
import { button, wireButtons, rect } from "game-kit"
const undo = button("undo", {
bounds: rect(1.8, 0.66),
surface: "ui/plate", face: "ui/face", inset: 0.05,   // a ring, because two strokes need two nodes
label: t("actions.undo"), style: "ui/label",         // YOUR words, already written
means: { does: "undo" },                             // what a press means — data
shadow: "silhouette",
const stop = wireButtons({ host, onPress: (meaning) => run(meaning["does"]) })
## The wiring the kit owns
Everywhere else the kit hands over three functions (`glassOf`, `toUnits`, `pick`) and refuses to
write the twenty lines around them, because what a gesture MEANS is the game's business — a tap
on a card is an auto-move in one game and a bid in another. A button is the exception: "the
finger came down on me and went up on me" means the same thing in every game there will be.
So `wireButtons` exists, and it is deliberately not a gesture recogniser. No drag, no double-tap,
no long press: a control wanting those is a control whose meaning is the game's again. Nothing is
registered per control either — the tree is asked who is under the pointer at the moment there is
one, so a bar may be rebuilt every frame and never re-wired.
## There is no `variant`
A primary and a danger button are two registered SURFACES, and the switch between them is a name
on a field — the kit reads no sorts. That is what makes a fifth look cost a registration rather
than a branch in the preset.
docs.hudButton.bar: A row of controls, each one a `button()` literal. Every field on the panel is the spec's: change
`inset` to see the ring the second node draws, take `face` away to get a one-node button back,
and set `sink` or `nudge` to nothing to feel the difference between depth and displacement.
